name: United Kingdom
eligibility: The sources checked for this page describe the route to parenthood rather than who may use it, so this page does not state eligibility criteria. Who can apply for a parental order, and on what conditions, is set out in the legislation and needs confirming with a lawyer in the relevant part of the UK.
paymentModel: Intended parents may reimburse the surrogate's reasonable expenses. Paying anything more than reasonable expenses must be authorised by the family court before a parental order can be made. Advertising for, or as, a surrogate is illegal under the Surrogacy Arrangements Act 1985. A report by Surrogacy UK, cited by HFEA, records surrogates as typically reimbursed 10,000 to 15,000 pounds.
parentage: The surrogate is the legal mother at birth unless a parental order is obtained. A written arrangement is not legally binding, and the Law Commission's reform proposals keep arrangements unenforceable. Intended parents have to wait until the child is born and then apply to court, a process the Commission describes as typically taking six months to a year.

facts.claim: A written surrogacy arrangement can be made but is not legally binding, the surrogate is the legal mother unless a parental order is obtained, and payment is limited to the surrogate's reasonable expenses.

source.label: Surrogacy (treatment information)
source.supports: Regulator page. Note its publication date: it was written in 2016 and is used here for the basic legal structure, which is set by statute rather than by this page.

facts.claim: A parental order makes the intended parents the legal parents; paying more than reasonable expenses must be authorised by the family court before a parental order can be made; advertising for or as a surrogate is illegal under the Surrogacy Arrangements Act 1985.

source.label: Surrogacy: a factsheet
source.supports: The regulator's own factsheet, and the source of the reimbursement range quoted below, which it attributes to a Surrogacy UK report.

facts.claim: Surrogacy arrangements would remain unenforceable under the proposed reform, intended parents have to wait until the child is born and then apply to court, and the process typically takes six months to a year.

source.label: Surrogacy (law reform project)
source.publisher: Law Commission of England and Wales, with the Scottish Law Commission
source.supports: Project page recording the 2023 report and draft Bill, the government's interim response of 8 November 2023, and a letter of 10 April 2025 stating the government is unable to prioritise surrogacy reform currently. The draft Bill is not law.

facts.claim: Surrogacy UK Foundation is entered on the register of charities in England and Wales with purposes covering information, advice and guidance about access to safe and ethical surrogacy, awareness-raising among healthcare professionals, lawyers and social workers, and support for research.

source.label: Charity detail: SURROGACYUK FOUNDATION (no. 1205088)
source.publisher: Charity Commission for England and Wales
source.supports: Public register entry, with financial year data to 31 December 2025. Registration records the organisation's purposes. It does not mean the organisation is regulated for surrogacy activity, and HFEA supervision covers licensed treatment clinics, not surrogacy support organisations.

openQuestions: Surrogacy law in Scotland and Northern Ireland differs from England and Wales. This page is not a statement about those systems.

The Law Commission's draft Bill has not been enacted. The government's position as recorded on the project page is that reform is not currently prioritised, which may have changed since the April 2025 letter.
Whether your existing arrangement or a foreign order would be recognised in the UK is a separate legal question this page does not address.
No UK total-cost figure was verified. The only sourced number is the reimbursement range for expenses above, which comes from an organisation's report rather than an official dataset.
